articles.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
articles.snippet: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
articles.full_text:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

- Published2 hours ago
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
'Brainstorming process'
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
'Endless betrayal'
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "Â£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.snippet: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
articles.full_text:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near MoÅodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa DÄba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
articles.snippet: Russia launched one of its biggest air attacks yet as it rejected the prospect of security guarantees for Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
- Published
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit â¬70bn (Â£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
articles.snippet: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday.
Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT).

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.
“Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.
Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively.
Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent.
More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.
Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.

articles.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
articles.snippet: Police officials called for "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
articles.full_text:
Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
- Published
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.
This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.
The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.
In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.
The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.
The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.
Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.
It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.
Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published19 September
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.
The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.
The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.
On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.
General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.
The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.
The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.
He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.
Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.
In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.
Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.snippet: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
articles.full_text:
Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
- Published
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.
A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.
Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.
Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.
Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.
When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".
He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."
Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.
"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"
The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.
Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
articles.snippet: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
articles.full_text:
Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
- Published
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.
US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".
India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.
At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.
"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.
In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

articles.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
articles.snippet: Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year in Anton Chekhov's play, The Seagull, in the US.
articles.full_text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
- Published
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.
Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.
Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.
But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".
During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.
"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.
"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.
Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".
"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.
Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".
"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.
She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."
Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.
She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.
The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.
Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".
"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.
Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.
Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.
"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.
"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.
"The Gower Peninsula is breathtaking."
She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".
"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map.
“The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence
- list 2 of 4‘Groundbreaking’ Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Five key takeaways
- list 3 of 4Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
- list 4 of 4Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations
“Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation.
It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine.
“The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.”
On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span.
During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week.
On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge.
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.”
Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”.
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”.
On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway.
In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky.
“Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said.
Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport.
Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active.
Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place.
Defying two superpowers
Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous.
“The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.
This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On November 6, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13.
For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it.
During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel.
Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.
US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have reportedly threatened Ukraine with an intelligence cutoff if it continues to strike Russian refineries.
As Ukraine defied them, Putin and Trump took to the global stage as the guests of Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the city of Shenzhen on November 19.
It was the first time Putin and Trump had met since their summit in Alaska in August 2025, and the first time all three men had met.
Kremlin-aligned media made much of the event, picking up Putin’s comparison with the Big Three conference in Yalta at the end of the second world war.
“The world’s three most consequential powers – have met. As the Big Three, they have emerged as the principal force in shaping a new architecture for international and European security,” wrote Putin’s deputy on the National Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev. “Today … no-one needs Europe.”
Asked whether peace in Ukraine was any closer as a result of the summit, Putin said he and Trump were still aligned on the proposals they discussed in Alaska. Those involved Ukraine handing over to Russia the one-fifth of the eastern Donbas region it cannot take by force, and to agree not to join NATO.
In the recent negotiations at Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, Ukraine was reportedly offered a green light to join NATO in return for the Donbas.
At those talks, Russia also turned its emphasis on Europe’s future security architecture.
Putin developed this further in Shenzhen, reported The New York Times and Bild magazine. He apparently offered Kremlin approval of Ukraine’s EU membership as long as Ukraine did not become part of EU defence policy, and as long as the United Kingdom and France refrained from offering a pan-European nuclear deterrent.
It would be “strange to discuss Europe’s security without Europe itself,” Putin said. On Ukraine’s however, he appeared to demand Europe sign onto whatever the US and Russia agreed.
Despite US and Russian attempts to appear to rearrange the world order, Europe did not appear to be listening.
During the past week, it provided Ukraine with a tranche of 1.7 billion euros ($1.97bn) from a 90 billion euros ($104.4bn) Ukraine Support Loan agreed in 2025, and another 8 billion euros ($9.28bn) from the Ukraine Facility, a 50 billion euros ($58bn) fund focused on Ukrainian economic recovery and financial support.
In addition to these two facilities, the EU agreed this week to raise 45 billion euros ($52.2bn), covering most of a 70-billion-euro ($81.2bn) shortfall that Ukraine says it will face next year. Of that amount, 25 billion euros ($29bn) will be for additional military assistance.
In addition to being a staunch supporter of Ukraine, however, Europe continued to be a divided supporter, deciding that its top diplomat should not represent it in talks with Russia and Ukraine, but representatives from its five biggest economies instead.
Kaja Kallas has argued that “all the member states actually agreed that I am the one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy” when they appointed her to the job of chief of the External Action Service.
“We have institutions in place so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending,” she said this week, in a clear reference to Witkoff and Kushner. “Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation.
The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Mamdani: ‘it’s morning again in America’ after blue wave
- list 2 of 3Zohran Mamdani’s influence grows as Democrats eye 2028 strategies
- list 3 of 3New York Democratic Socialists urge Ocasio-Cortez to run for US president
With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction.
The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said.
How does Mamdani plan to close Rikers Island?
The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays.
Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence.
Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs.
“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city.
Why is Rikers Island notorious?
Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade.
The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release.
City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration.
Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change.
“Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

articles.title: Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

articles.full_text:
Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.
Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4‘What’s wrong with citizens taking to the streets with a Palestinian flag?’

Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages and greater investment in public services.
The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare.
“Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome.
Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump.
The Italian rallies followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations.
Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry.
Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education.
Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it was organising protests in 73 cities and towns.
In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s Alexanderplatz square.
The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said.
Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service.
In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.
In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.
Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting.
On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency.
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws.
A top Democrat, who will wield significant investigative powers in the United States Congress starting in January, has warned US law enforcement agencies to preserve records, including encrypted communications on digital messaging apps.
In letters sent on Thursday to the US Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the next likely chairman of the US House Judiciary Committee, wrote to the cabinet-level agencies to remind their employees of a legal obligation to “safeguard” records against destruction.

Letters were also sent to the heads of three subagencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Prisons (BOP).
Raskin disclosed he has obtained evidence that government officials in the Trump administration have been using non-government apps, like Signal, to send disappearing messages.
The Maryland Democrat, who is currently the Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, appended a screenshot of a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of President Donald Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, showing a conversation where messages were set to automatically delete after one week.
“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records”, Raskin wrote to US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.”
The incident, Raskin wrote, is “just one of many” that have been reported to the Judiciary Committee, raising concern among Democrats that the Trump administration could be ignoring federal recordkeeping laws by destroying documents before likely congressional investigations.
“There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records”, Raskin wrote. “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials”.
Raskin instructed the federal officials to take “immediate action to recover these records” from data backups or “associated metadata,” asking them to comply by December 3.
The Trump administration has signalled it intends to fight any probes by US Democrats, who won control of both chambers of the US Congress earlier this month in the country’s midterm elections.
According to a letter viewed by Al Jazeera, the White House’s top lawyer, Will Scharf, wrote to US House Democrats on Wednesday, pushing back against demands from the incoming Democratic majorities, such as Raskin’s, because the new Congress has not yet been sworn in.
“Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated,” Scharf wrote. “As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e] … the needs of the conflicting branches'”.
In response to Raskin’s letter, a White House official told Al Jazeera the administration complies “with all federal record retention laws and regulations”.
The DOJ echoed the White House’s response, saying it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.”
“The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent'”, the agency said about Raskin.
Al Jazeera also reached out to DHS, FBI, ICE and BOP for comment but has not yet heard back.

UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK.
A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom.
Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board.
Recommended Stories
