- list 2 of 3‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism
- list 3 of 3Child among three killed off French coast in Channel crossing attempt
Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel.
“They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added.
Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred onto another vessel and taken ashore.
The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident.
Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the boat … take them back, no more of these”.
‘Thuggish’
Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of the incident was played.
Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate attempt to disrupt rescue efforts.
The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats.
A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”.
The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping.
Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March.
UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

articles.title: 10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
articles.full_text:
10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.
For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
- list 2 of 4Andy Burnham says Brexit is what the UK’s ‘enemies’ wanted
- list 3 of 4Britain’s Brexit woes: ‘I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did’
- list 4 of 4EU and UK agree a reset deal to end ‘decade of drift’
Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.
As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician, a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.
Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.
The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.
On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.
The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.
Does the UK want to rejoin?
Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.
According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.
“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.
Could the UK Breturn?
According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.
However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.
“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.
“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”
Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.
Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.
While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.
“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.
Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.
Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.
“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.
“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did: immigration.
“If Burnham is going to try to get the sort of energy he’ll need to see the process through, he’s going to need to do something similar, though what, I don’t know.”

articles.title: Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says
articles.snippet: The agreement was among the major achievements of Trump's trip to Asia, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, even as the two countries compete for AI supremacy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday.
Bessent told CNBC after returning from Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, China, that the agreement was among the major achievements of Trump’s trip to Asia.
“I think it was very important that President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent said, referring to the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology, “super intelligence.”
Bessent said that the U.S.-China agreement on military use of the technology, requiring human involvement and other safeguards, would not be affected by the two countries’ competition for AI supremacy. He added that U.S. AI labs needed to maintain their technological lead as the best defense against “dangerous” Chinese AI models that are being used in cyberattacks.
“But there’s nothing to do with competition when it says that both sides agree that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved,” Bessent said.
He said that the spying allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national that he was romantically involved with did not come up in the Trump-Xi bilateral meeting.
Bessent said that Nvidia’s second-tier AI chip, the H200, remained the most advanced chip that China could purchase with licenses, after Trump took what he called a “very firm line.”
“I think what we have seen is a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s as they try to build out their own chip stack, and I think that they are probably many years behind,” he added.
Bessent downplayed differences that he had voiced between the views of Treasury and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on AI chip restrictions in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, saying Trump administration officials were “all committed to following President Trump’s instructions.”
The Commerce Department took steps on Monday to further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, including those used by overseas data centers where Chinese entities can rent computing power.
“I think we are going to see that the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed,” he said.

articles.title: German attack drones pass live-fire tests, with first deliveries planned this year
articles.snippet: Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
articles.full_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
Though the systems have yet to complete qualification, the German Army plans to begin equipping its armored brigade in Lithuania in 2027.
The trials, held the week of Nov. 9, tested whether Stark’s Virtus and Helsing’s HX-2 could reliably hit designated targets and whether their warheads worked as intended on impact. The Bundeswehr conducted key parts of the testing at its weapons and ammunition test center in Meppen. The procurement office announced that both systems passed but did not disclose how many shots it fired or the weapons’ success rates.
Photos attached to the statement showed both an OWE-V Virtus and an HX-2 loitering munition moments before impact into a tank.
Both systems are loitering munitions, weapons that can remain airborne over an area while searching for targets before a human operator decides whether to authorize a strike. The live-fire campaign focused on the final part of that process, from the approach to the target through the effect of the warhead, rather than certifying the systems for service.
The military noted that before loitering munitions can be used within the German Armed Forces, they must be thoroughly tested on the “interaction of the various system components.”
German lawmakers were previously skeptical of approving armed drones for the country’s military, and some arms control researchers have raised concerns about autonomous targeting in loitering munitions.
The tests follow a Feb. 25 vote by Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approving contracts worth €268 million ($294.4 million) apiece for Stark and Helsing. Options could add €1 billion to each deal, but further purchases depend on the systems proving technologically mature and lawmakers approving the spending, Defense News reported in February. The vote marked a shift that’s part of a larger rethinking of Germany’s military posture in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Germany is trying to shorten the time between signing a contract and getting the weapons to troops by allowing concurrent development, testing, qualification and preparations for use. The procurement office said it brought soldiers into testing early so their feedback could inform changes to the systems. Lawmakers attached reporting requirements to the spending plan, and cancellation clauses allow the government to walk away if a system fails qualification.
The procurement office said it expects initial deliveries this year so troops can begin training. It did not say how many weapons would arrive in that first batch. The army intends eventually to link the munitions with its reconnaissance and strike systems, with the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania slated to become the first major formation to receive them starting in 2027.

articles.title: Dutch defense-industry plan targets 40% growth, €15 billion revenue by 2030
articles.snippet: The nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several key defense technology areas.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 billion ($16.5 billion).
The government has earmarked €1.6 billion for the industry plan, with a focus on integrated air and missile defense, data-driven command and digital resilience, unmanned and autonomous systems; and military sustainment.
The Netherlands is the seventh-biggest defense spender among European NATO countries, ahead of Sweden, based on data from the alliance, yet the country lacks major defense prime comparable to Sweden’s Saab, Germany’s Rheinmetall or the United Kingdom’s BAE Systems.
Still, the nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several defense technology areas. For example, France’s Thales has a large part of its radar business in the Netherlands, while the country is also home to Destinus, a defense technology company which said this week its Ruta cruise missiles were used by Ukraine to target the Kerch Strait bridge.
“Through this national program, the government, together with industry and research institutions, is rolling up its sleeves to ensure that the armed forces get what they need, both now and in a conflict situation,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
Warfighting is fundamentally changing, and the impact of technology is “enormous,” the government said, citing space technology, the electromagnetic spectrum, artificial intelligence, cyber, drones and long-range weapons. At the same time, the war in Ukraine has shown the importance of mass, production capability, stocks and the ability to sustain the fight, according to the government.
Strengthening the Dutch defense industry will strengthen the warfighting ability of the Dutch armed forces, according to the government. Spending on the plan will include €600 million for industrial ecosystems and scaling production, €320 million to help pay for international cooperation, and €150 million on make supply chains more resilient.
The Netherlands is counting on the domestic share of Dutch defense-industry revenue to grow faster than the industry’s overall revenue, climbing 50% by 2030 to more than €10 billion. Meanwhile, the target is for exports to grow by about 25%.
The MoD will give greater weight to the origin of products and suppliers in procurement decisions in 2027, and introduce procurement guidelines from the first quarter of 2028 that take into account the origin of raw materials and components, as well a supply-chain transparency, the government said.
The Netherlands is betting on international cooperation in the focus areas, and will actively contribute to leading groups for joint capability development with like-minded partners including Belgium, Germany, France, the U.K. and the Nordic countries, the government said.
“Thanks to their innovative capacity, the Dutch defense industry and research institutions are in a good position to play key roles in global value chains and in this way help reduce risky strategic dependencies for the Netherlands and Europe,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
To improve financing access for defense firms, the Ministry of Defence together with Invest-NL will set up a €200 million investment fund for dual-use companies in defense and security.
The MoD will also set up the National Institute for Defence Technology, or NIDT, in 2028, with a budget that will climb to €350 million a year by 2030, the government said. The goal of the new institute will be to accelerate innovation and scaling up.
The government plans to strengthen protections against unwanted takeovers and investments in strategically important Dutch defense companies, as well as against leaks of sensitive technology and expertise, with a target to have additional legal instruments in place from 2028.

articles.title: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows
articles.snippet: A new CSIS report warns that the Iran war has strained US missile stockpiles, raising concerns about America's readiness for a potential conflict with China.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The report analyzed data on munitions expenditures that were current as of November 3 to provide estimates of how missile usage against Iran is affecting U.S. defense posture globally.
“In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories,” according to the report.
It points out that, while the Pentagon has made agreements with manufacturers to boost production rates and Congress may provide funding, time is of the essence to rebuild the U.S. arsenal, as the current strain on stockpiles has created vulnerabilities.
“Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis,” the analysis notes.
CSIS produced a list of missile types sorted into nine categories. Seven of the nine categories were classed as having “detrimental effects” in terms of resupply capacity.
According to this analysis, Patriot missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, and Standard Missiles, which are vertically launched surface-to-air missiles, are listed as “heavily used, no substitutes,” indicating that stockpiles are in dire condition.
Long-range ground-attack missiles including Tomahawks, AGM-158 JASSM cruise missiles, and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) are described as being “heavily used” with “some substitutes.”
The only missile types listed as having “no significant constraints in most scenarios” are short-range munitions – including air-to-air missiles and short- and medium-range missiles, including GBU-39B small-diameter bombs and the AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is primed to strike low-altitude targets.
CSIS observes that, while the U.S. is still capable of leveraging existing missiles against targets in the short term, shortages of long-range munitions create operational challenges.
“The United States has large numbers of munitions with the same explosive yield and accuracy as the long-range systems described above but with ranges under 300 miles,” according to the report.
The U.S. is at risk of losing its ability to project power through ballistics across long distances.
At the same time, munitions with shorter ranges increase the importance of establishing air superiority. This could create complexities if the U.S. faces a powerful adversary that has sufficient air power and defenses to fend off shorter-range weapons and prevent them from being effective.
“Although production rates are increasing, demand exceeds supply—from both the United States and allies—so timelines have lengthened,” the report warns. “The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.”

articles.title: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict
articles.snippet: Denmark's parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future.
articles.full_text:
Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island’s future that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.
“This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement posted on X.
The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark’s foreign ministry tells the U.S. in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the U.S. Senate.
It expands the US military’s role in Greenland, including permission to establish a “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security grounds and plans for two new US military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark’s Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters.
“I expect that the U.S. will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and the arrangement around these two areas,” he said.
Trump’s refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and months of intensive negotiations.
Difficult time for Greenlanders
Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, said Trump’s pressure had led to distrust in Greenland towards the U.S. administration.
“It’s been really difficult for Greenlanders these past two years. It’s been seeping into every aspect of our lives,” Nathanielsen told Reuters. She hoped the agreement would open a path to dialogue after hurtful rhetoric within the Western alliance.
Greenland’s parliament ratified the deal this month. Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize the situation in Greenland.
Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, said the deal was more likely a beginning than an end.
“With the treaty in hand, the U.S. will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on part of the extraction of strategic resources,” he said.
Other experts say the new agreement does not add much U.S. military access to Greenland. The northernmost U.S. base is already in Greenland, which lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America.
Trump last month said that “massive oil, gas and mineral exploration” was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has banned new drilling for crude. Denmark has said any resource extraction must respect local law.

articles.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
articles.snippet: “DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
articles.full_text:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.
The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.
“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”
The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026. Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”
Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs.
The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after
shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.
Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs.
The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO said.
“DOD is taking steps to increase production in response to real shortages,” Diana Moldafsky, a director of GAO’s Defense Capabilities and Management team, told Defense News. “That said, we found some cases where DOD increased production in response to immediate shortages without basing the increase on its total requirement for that munition.”
Nor does the Pentagon have a good grasp on how much ammunition it actually has.
Each military service has its data system to track munitions inventories, which is then aggregated by DoD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative to provide, in theory, a near real-time glimpse of stockpiles as well as supply chain links.
“In total, MRI pulls from 37 DOD data sources through a mix of automated connections and some manually updated data,” GAO noted.
However, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment “does not consistently reconcile MRI munitions inventory data against the services’ own data systems.” Nor does it have “a data management plan detailing how data is aggregated in the MRI tool from across the services.”
“MRI does aggregate from the individual services’ data systems, but we found instances where the numbers in the tool differed from the services’ databases,” said Moldafsky.
Authority over munitions inventories is also fragmented among multiple offices within the DoD and the program executive offices in individual services. Working groups that are supposed to bring them together lack authority and accountability.
All of which points to the root of the problem: no one is really in charge. “DoD has not identified an office or entity and delegated to it authority that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories departmentwide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels,” the GAO report notes.
GAO recommended that DoD create an overarching plan to match munitions requirements, production and funding, as well as metrics to track progress. Without it, the report warns, the “DoD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.”

articles.title: France and Sweden hold first joint nuclear-deterrence exercise
articles.snippet: The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A330 MRTT tanker aircraft operating over Sweden alongside Swedish Gripen fighters.
The exercise, dubbed Excalibur, was held in northern Sweden on Nov. 16 to 18, with the aim of improving interoperability between the French and Swedish air forces, the two countries’ armed forces said in statements on Thursday. The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
The French-Swedish cooperation follows an exercise last month in which British Eurofighter Typhoon jets escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission. France has been working with several European allies to implement Macron’s proposal to bolster European deterrence, in the face of nuclear saber-rattling by Russia and uncertainty about United States security guarantees.
France’s nuclear deterrent consists of an ocean-based component comprising strategic ballistic-missile submarines, as well as an airborne component consisting of Rafale jets capable of carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles developed by MBDA.
“Since the in-depth dialogue on ‘forward deterrence’ was initiated, France and Sweden are taking steps to implement their common roadmap for strategic cooperation,” the Swedish Armed Forces said. The exercise “demonstrates our joint readiness and capability to act together and reflects the commitment of our two countries towards deterring threats and strengthening allied security.”
The deployment of the Rafale jets alongside Gripen fighters, with the support of an A330 MRTT, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the two air forces in the areas of nuclear deterrence, in the service of Europe’s security, the French Armed Forces General Staff said in a post on the social network X.
“This type of deployment not only allows to test the dispersion of French aircraft to improve their capability to survive an adversary disabling strike, but also opens the door for new modes of operation previously unimaginable, such as attacking targets deep within the Russian Arctic or planning much smaller raids without needing in-flight refueling,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X.
Sweden’s Gripen fighters are “excellent combat aircraft” specifically designed to penetrate Russian ground-to-air and air-to-air defense systems, and they could be valuable assets during a nuclear strike mission, while freeing up conventional Rafale jets for other missions, Marcuz said.

articles.title: Autonomy firm Auterion to launch joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Skyfall
articles.snippet: The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, will produce Skyfall drones with Auterion software in Germany, “outside the range of air strikes,” Auterion said.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — American autonomous software firm Auterion and Ukrainian drone producer Skyfall plan to form a joint venture to “manufacture drones for Ukraine at high volume in a new factory in Germany,” Auterion announced today.
The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, “is being established under the auspices of the official ‘Build with Ukraine’ defense cooperation framework,” the announcement said.
According to Auterion, “initial production” by the joint venture will “focus on the Shrike FPV platform” and is expected to later expand to Skyfall interceptors as well as middle- and deep-strike systems. “Every drone combines a Skyfall airframe with Auterion avionics” as well as Auterion’s operating system, the company said.
Auterion and Skyfall previously partnered for drone production for Ukraine, but Auterion said today that a German factory in particular “adds production capacity outside the range of air strikes, while maintaining a knowledge link and short innovation cycle available to Skyfall’s engineers.
“Feedback from units at the front reaches those engineers every week and goes straight into the German line,” the company said.
Auterion, which is based in Munich as well as the US, said the agreement was inked during the German-Ukrainian Economic Forum today, and Reuters reported that the German government would provide funding for the new factory and for drone orders. Citing an industry official, the newswire reported the funding would be in the range of hundreds of millions of euros first to provide drones to Ukraine and then to the German armed forces.
“SkyFall and Auterion have put more than 50,000 drones into the hands of Ukrainian units with advanced terminal guidance and target detection” Lorenz Meier, founder and CEO of Auterion, said in the announcement. “A factory in Germany gives German forces a domestic source for the same drones Ukrainian units rely on every week.”

articles.title: Sweden’s Nordic Air Defence launches K200 drone interceptor, pushes toward Ukraine tests
articles.snippet: The Swedish firm said that the counter-drone solution, a successor to the Kreuger 100XR, is designed to intercept jet-powered types, including the Russian Geran-3a.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — Swedish start up Nordic Air Defence (NAD) has unveiled an autonomous drone interceptor, dubbed K200 and destined for testing in Ukraine.
The Scandinavian firm said in a company statement today that the counter-unmanned aerial system (cUAS) weapon, a successor to the company’s Kreuger 100XR, is designed to intercept jet-powered types, including the Russian Geran-3a.
“NAD has opened a staffed office in Ukraine, where testing will inform further development of the K200 as the company prepares to introduce the system across multiple markets,” noted the statement.
It added that the system has been engineered in Stockholm and is built to intercept long-range attack drones “at a fraction of the cost of conventional air defence missiles, helping armed forces scale their defences as attacks grow in volume, speed, and accuracy.”
The announcement claims the K200 is both faster and capable of carrying a heavier, 500g (approximately 1 lb.) warhead compared to the older Kreuger 100XR. The system is also integrated with autonomous guidance, with a single-propeller and fixed wing design.
Additionally, a number of external radars and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) cameras allow the interceptor to fly toward a threat, before it relies on terminal guidance provided by an onboard IR camera for “final approach.” Should a target be missed, the interceptor can also “re-engage.”
The new weapon “supports tail-chase, head-on and crossing engagements and is designed to integrate with existing layered air defence systems through data links and associated radars,” the announcement outlined. The company said a family of launchers could support deployments from vehicles, fixed sites and vessels.
Drone interceptors are in high demand worldwide, but especially in Ukraine as it routinely faces barrages of Russian one way attack drones. Besides K200 trials in Ukraine, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times last month that Kyiv is testing five locally produced jet-powered drone interceptors.
Overnight, Moscow launched a wave of over 400 attack drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, he noted on X today. He said that 79 cruise missiles had been shot down, but looking at ballistic missiles, “unfortunately, it is much more difficult, and that now depends not on our forces but on our partners supplying missiles.”
Ukraine generally relies on more expensive and sophisticated air defense missiles to combat incoming ballistic missiles, but a shortage of American-made Patriot interceptors has strained Kyiv’s ability to fend off Russia’s onslaughts.

articles.title: Trump to keynote Reagan National Defense Forum
articles.snippet: Trump will be the first president to attend the RNDF, which has steadily grown in size over the years.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump will give a keynote speech at the annual Reagan National Defense Forum, becoming the first president to speak at the event.
Trump’s speech is scheduled for 3:00 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday Dec. 4. The vast majority of Reagan’s programming is held the next day, meaning Trump will have a solo spotlight to address the crowd.
The RNDF, held at the Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, Calif., has steadily grown as a key defense event year over year. While drawing leadership from the Pentagon and traditional defense industry, it has emerged as the hub for the California-based defense tech startup scene — of which many have politically aligned themselves with the Trump administration.
Trump’s speech could provide an interesting contrast to the main day programing, where democratic lawmakers are expected to appear on panels and do interviews outlining their plans for the new Congress.

articles.title: One data foundation and many application layers drive the Army’s NGC2 transformation
articles.snippet: Across the Indo-Pacific, the Army is testing how shared data and open systems can speed battlefield decisions.
articles.full_text:
The Army’s Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) effort rests on a simple premise: the service can no longer afford C2 systems that can’t talk to one another, take years to update, or fail when an adversary jams a link. Those issues become particularly glaring when viewed in the light of operations across a theater as vast as the Indo-Pacific.
The Army’s answer is a shared data foundation with applications layered on top, replacing the separate, platform-specific systems that now serve fires, air defense, and logistics. Each piece is built so it can be swapped out while maintaining interoperability with the rest.
At its core, NGC2 is about “shifting the paradigm to a mission-centric operation,” said Chandra Marshall, vice president, programs, enterprise operations at Lockheed Martin. The Army wants a composable architecture with common applications and core services, she said, enabling integration of new software, weapons, and sensors without rework and knocking down silos at every echelon.
A threat picture that punishes stovepipes
The case for that shift starts with the electromagnetic spectrum. Josh Wallin, a defense program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, points to Ukraine, where Russian forces jam, interfere with, and track electromagnetic spectrum emissions. The US hasn’t faced an enemy that targets the spectrum so heavily, and the risk to communications and data links between Army forces grows against a capable adversary in the Indo-Pacific, he said.
Then there is geography. Neither the Global War on Terror, nor the current fight in Iran, nor even the war in Ukraine has required the Army to connect systems that might sit thousands of miles apart, Wallin said. Commercial infrastructure could fill some gaps, although relying on cellular networks would be more difficult. Satellite communications could offer another means of connectivity.
Bandwidth may prove the harder constraint. The Army, Navy, and Air Force are all pursuing distributed operating concepts, which assume scattered units will continually pass data among nodes to stay synchronized. With less massing of forces in a few locations, that data has to travel farther and over more contested paths.
Speed adds pressure, and in Ukraine, “we might be talking on the order of minutes from acquisition to servicing a target,” Wallin said.
The problem exists inside individual warfighting functions, too. For air defense, only recently have Patriot and THAAD been able to cue each other, with a THAAD radar controlling a Patriot interceptor. Layered defense can’t work if each system fights alone, Wallin argued. It’s “super inefficient,” he said, and against a large volume of incoming threats, stovepiped units may simply be unable to share information fast enough to coordinate a response.
The data layer is the foundation
The NGC2 data layer ingests information and makes it available to any application or operator according to role, access level, and warfighting function, Marshall explained. The Army sets the rules, and the system uses them to determine who needs a given piece of data and at what level of the force it should go.
This is a key challenge for NGC2 because air defense, logistics, and fires each run their own data and communications infrastructure. Centralizing data across them, according to Wallin, will give logisticians trying to sustain distributed forces visibility into ongoing operations, the threat picture, and intelligence feeds that once lived in separate systems.
Pooling the data is the first step. The next is drawing conclusions about how information across functions relate. The 25th Infantry Division in Hawaii has been the experimental unit charged with demonstrating the approach, with Lockheed Martin serving as the Full Stack Operational Implementation Lead.
During Lightning Surge 3 in April, the team fused sensors, fires systems, and airspace data into a single cloud-enabled picture, according to Marshall. She called it the first demonstration of cross-domain data sharing in the 25th ID environment, working across multiple locations that spanned Hawaii, the Philippines, and the broader Indo-Pacific. The outcome was a shared real-time view and compressed sensor-to-shooter timeline, she said.
The NGC2 program is also changing how the Army develops and fields C2 software. Rather than giving industry a fixed set of technical requirements, the Army established operational objectives that could be refined as soldiers used the systems. That has allowed developers to incorporate feedback directly from the field instead of waiting for the next major upgrade cycle.
“They give us feedback real time so we can make software changes within minutes, hours, days, depending on the complexity of the feature,” Marshall said. “When we conduct Lightning Surges, it’s about operational fight-tonight capability the 25th ID can use now. It’s not a prototype, so it’s been powerful in that regard.”
One example came during Lightning Surge 4, when soldiers wanted to operate the system without having to interact physically with a screen. Developers responded by integrating an AI-driven hand microphone with an Army edge device, allowing soldiers to issue spoken commands instead of touching. The capability was designed, built, and delivered within days, according to Marshall.
The approach represents a departure from programs in which requirements are established years before soldiers receive the resulting capabilities. Marshall said the team delivered NGC2 solutions in less than 10 months that the 25th ID used operationally across the Pacific and exercised during Balikatan, the annual US-Philippine military exercise.
AI as an aid, not a decider
Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the applications layered on top of the data foundation, though both Marshall and Wallin were careful about how much weight to put on it. AI can comb through available data and turn it around to commanders quickly, cutting latency from minutes to seconds, according to Marshall. However, it is one tool among several, and it isn’t making decisions for the Army. It correlates data and offers recommendations so commanders have the right information at the right time. The decision aids already demonstrated are “very powerful,” she said.
The practical hope for AI, in Wallin’s view, is to automate what can be automated and speed up tasks that are heavily manual today. Even “a 60 percent solution on something that was 100 percent manual before” could free operators to focus on other responsibilities, he said.
Another important feature of NGC2 is that its architecture is designed so its layers can be pulled apart and replaced independently. The Army is trying to separate the physical data links, meaning which cable runs to which radio and which satellite, from the compute infrastructure, and to separate both from the software that manages the data, Wallin said. Soldiers interact with the application layers on top.
If an adversary finds a new way to jam or track something like a satellite terminal, the Army could replace that hardware with something less vulnerable without disturbing everything above it. Advances in computing power and the shrinking size of computing hardware could give the Army more room to accommodate future applications. More importantly, the service is moving away from the assumption that software and hardware acquired today must remain in service for decades.
The goal is to create an architecture that can continuously evolve as adversaries develop new methods of disrupting communications, targeting military networks, and exploiting vulnerabilities. Instead of replacing an entire C2 system, the Army could update individual components while preserving the larger data infrastructure.
Building a C2 ecosystem that evolves
Implementation of the Army’s Modular Open Systems Approach to NGC2 also makes it easier to move beyond specific suppliers and systems when they underperform or aren’t pacing evolving threats with improvements. At the 25th ID, Lockheed Martin runs what Marshall called a strict onboarding and offboarding process, evaluating each element with the Army to decide whether it is the right fit for its piece of the architecture.
That differs from traditional acquisition programs in which a single prime contractor may control much of the system and replacing a supplier can mean extensive integration work. By establishing common interfaces and services, the Army is attempting to make competition and continuous upgrades part of the architecture itself.
The ecosystem is already large. More than 60 companies have contributed to the Army’s NGC2 effort or are under analysis for it, Marshall said, including small businesses, nontraditional innovators, and commercial-technology providers. The 25th ID’s data platform is based on Raft’s Raft Data Platform. Amazon Web Services supplies Wickr Chat, a communications and collaboration tool. Rune Technologies delivered TyrOS for contested logistics.
For the Army, the larger test will be whether the approach demonstrated by the 25th ID can be extended to other formations without recreating the stovepipes NGC2 was designed to eliminate. The ongoing Lightning Surge exercises and the 4th Infantry Division’s Ivy Sting exercises at Fort Carson represent opportunities to evaluate how common data infrastructure, modular applications, and soldier-driven software development can support different operational requirements.
The stakes are particularly high in the Indo-Pacific, where formations will be separated by thousands of miles and forced to operate with intermittent comms. A shared architecture will not eliminate those constraints, but it could give commanders the ability to exploit available data, change communications equipment, and incorporate new capabilities without rebuilding the entire C2 network.

articles.title: Pentagon CIO Davies tapped as acting National Cyber Director
articles.snippet: Kirsten Davies is taking over the role for Sean Cairncross at the White House.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies has assumed the role of National Cyber Director following the Thursday departure of Sean Cairncross, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed.
Davies also confirmed in a post on X that she would be moving into the White House role, which was created in 2021 to serve as the top advisor to the president on cyber matters and coordinate cyber activities and responses across the myriad government agencies.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” the post, shared from her personal account, reads. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future.”
It is not clear who is assuming the duties of Pentagon CIO, and the Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment by press time.
Davies takes over at a tense time in which several major cyber and IT incidents have raised alarm bells across the country, with outages ranging from air traffic control to airlines to banks to sensitive national security networks.
Prior to assuming the CIO role in December 2025, Davies served as the chief information security officer at Unilever.
Since taking office, she has stressed four key pillars in the job:
- supporting warfighting systems from IT, operational technology and Internet of Things devices;
- maturing digital capabilities such as speeding the delivery of software and standardizing data architectures;
- transforming cybersecurity; and
- up-skilling and cross-skilling the workforce.
Davies has also inked multiple large contracts under enterprise service agreements. For example, she signed one for Dell in May for $9.7 billion to consolidate Microsoft software, services and licenses across, and one for Oracle in July for $7 billion to consolidate “fragmented, one-off information technology purchases.”
One of the most controversial decisions she has made in her tenure was the suspension of the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification’s third-party assessments, which is what some experts refer to as the bedrock of the program. While the initial 60-day review window for the suspension has come and gone, there has not been any update regarding the status of the program or its suspension.

articles.title: Skylark Labs demonstrates humanoid search for explosive hazards
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] CFAM delivered about 30% higher task success than a standard model in a real-world robot test. Skylark is applying that learning approach to explosive-hazard search.
articles.full_text:
Searching suspected explosive ground puts people in danger. Skylark Labs has demonstrated a humanoid that can take on that search with a standard handheld metal detector—sweeping the ground and responding to its alert under human supervision. The aim is to keep explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) specialists farther from suspected hazards while they direct and assess the search.
In an experiment conducted for an EOD supplier, the robot picked up the detector, swept a designated search area and stopped and backed off when it sounded. It carried out the sequence without a separate command for each step.
Skylark says visual and audio feedback guided the robot through the task. The detector’s beep became an input to its next action, connecting what the machine sensed with what it did. Company footage shows the humanoid sweeping outdoors alongside a person performing the same search. The demo footage can be seen here.
“Our customers already own and trust their detectors. A robot that learns the search from the specialists who do it, and then runs it with that same equipment, takes people out of the most dangerous moments without handing them more work.”
EOD supplier representative
The threat is persistent. Action on Armed Violence recorded 10,376 IED incidents across 94 countries between 2015 and 2024, causing 83,529 civilian deaths and injuries. Suspected devices can also halt movement, restrict access and divert personnel.
EOD teams already rely on robots. In 2022, the U.S. Air Force began fielding 170 L3Harris T7 systems: tracked machines controlled by an operator. Skylark is pursuing a humanoid that carries out an assigned search without requiring a person to direct each movement.
The humanoid form is central to that approach. Its hands, reach and posture let it work with equipment designed for people, including the detectors EOD teams already carry. Learning to use those tools reduces the need to redesign equipment around a robot. The intended payoff is practical: less time spent directing a machine, and less human exposure at the front of the search.
Skylark’s Continual Field-Adaptive Models, or CFAMs, provide the learning capability. Specialists demonstrate how to handle familiar equipment and carry out a search. Skylark says the detector-search skill was taught through a few minutes of human demonstration. The models are designed to keep adapting on the device as the robot works, without a separate retraining cycle.
CFAM delivered about 30% higher task success than a standard model in a real-world manipulation test. In a separate evaluation, it matched a standard model’s performance using just 40% of the training data. It also learned new skills with little loss of earlier capabilities. Performance in new search conditions is still being tested.
“The first footsteps onto unswept ground carry the greatest risk. If a machine can reduce human risk while discerning the unknown, specialized judgment is reserved for the most complex challenges. That only works if we can readily summon machine sensing and human judgment for combined understanding that neither system can achieve alone.”
Retired U.S. Marine Corps Lt. Gen. Michael S. Groen, former director of the Pentagon’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center and a member of Skylark Labs’ Defense Advisory Board
The demonstrated work is detection support. Physical handling and disposal remain development goals. The humanoid’s value will depend on carrying out a defined search reliably enough that a specialist can supervise from greater separation, instead of being the first person onto unswept ground.
“Our mission is to enable machines—including humanoids—to independently carry out explosive ordnance disposal tasks, keeping people away from potentially lethal threats. We’re building the AI brain that allows these machines to learn efficiently and adapt to unfamiliar objects, terrain, and changing conditions, with the goal of making them reliable and effective in complex EOD operations,” said Amarjot Singh, Founder and CEO of Skylark Labs.
Skylark’s longer-term goal is a team of humanoids working together. Hive, its framework for coordinating multiple machines, is already deployed in oil and gas operations in the United States, India and the Middle East. Applied to EOD, it could let robots divide a search area, share findings and hand off work as conditions change, with one specialist overseeing the team.
The goal is to send the machine first, while keeping the specialist in charge.

articles.title: Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A China-linked threat actor used the open source AI penetration testing tool Cairn to persistently attack two universities, and in one case, possibly discover a zero-day bug, researchers said.
articles.full_text:
Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university
Chinese hackers used an AI tool called Cairn to allegedly discover a zero-day while breaching several universities in Asia, according to a new report from Amazon’s Threat Intelligence team.
CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said their investigation began on September 10, when they discovered a publicly accessible server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn — an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework.
They were able to view the operational history of the platform, including previous prompts and more. The operator wrote their prompts in Simplified Chinese and the timestamps were configured to China Standard Time. The targeted victim organizations were universities in East Asia.
Moses explained that Cairn is ideal for attackers because, when given a starting point and objective in plain language, it can coordinate multiple AI agents to complete a task.
In this incident, the attacker provided IP addresses and asked Cairn to “obtain shell access” — meaning find a way to gain enough access to a system for various actions to be taken.
“Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step,” Moses said.
One of the attempts involved 148 actions taken over 16 hours that were ultimately unsuccessful, including a failed attempt at exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability. Another failed effort saw Cairn try for more than six hours to breach university servers by testing more than 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames.
The only successful attempt occurred when the agents discovered a vulnerability in an open-source medical imaging AI application and exploited it.
“At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched,” Moses said.
“Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.”
The attacker then used the same apparent zero-day to breach a second university.
Moses said Amazon Threat Intelligence contacted the maintainers behind the open-source medical imaging AI application and they fixed the bug that was discovered.
He added that AWS “worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.” AWS declined to name the universities or the country they are in.
Moses said the campaign stood out because of the speed and operational tempo of the AI agents.
An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes “completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert,” Moses warned, noting that the agents “ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints.”
Artex vs. Cairn
Cybersecurity researchers and law enforcement agencies have released multiple warnings in recent weeks about AI-backed offensive cyber tools that are being used by attackers, particularly those from China.
The FBI published an advisory about AI tool Artex one week ago, writing that it could take any large language model and turn it into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.”
Artex was implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions while Microsoft said Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise. Moses said last week that Artex was seen used in credential theft attacks on AI models and in campaigns targeting crypto exchanges.
Cairn was also spotlighted by Google researchers on Tuesday in a report about the evolving use of autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI and others.
Google noted that it saw Cairn used in intrusions of companies in the U.S. aerospace sector and wrote, like AWS found, that it was adept at starting with a target’s IP address and ending with an operational objective.
The AWS report on Cairn cites a study released in September by cybersecurity firm Gambit Security that documented the use of Cairn by a financially motivated hacking group using the tool to breach online retailers.
Eyal Sela, Director of Threat Intelligence at Gambit Security and the researcher behind the report, told Recorded Future News that Cairn is more significant than Artex because it is a general-purpose tool.
“While it is good at solving ‘red team’ or capture-the-flag tasks, it can also solve other problems and the main point is that it has no internal structuring for cybersecurity,” Sela said.
“When a tool is more generic, it is less predictable because it has less structuring around the way it solves a task.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Hackers use autonomous AI tool Cairn to find zero-day, take over server
articles.snippet: Threat actors used the open-source AI penetration-testing framework Cairn to find a previously unknown vulnerability in a medical imaging application. [...]
articles.full_text:
Hackers used an autonomous AI agent platform called "Cairn" to discover a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application and exploit it to take complete control of a server.
According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, the suspected Chinese-linked attackers simply instructed the AI agents to "obtain shell access," leaving them to independently discover and exploit the flaw.
Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the campaign after discovering that the attackers had left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without authentication, exposing their hacking operations.
According to the researchers, the attacks were launched by a Chinese-nexus threat actor between September 8 and 10, 2026, targeting mainly East Asian educational institutions outside China.
Cairn is a legitimate pentesting tool that can be used to coordinate multiple AI agents in cyber-operations, created for research and defense strengthening.
Gambit Security documented cases of Cairn abuse as part of a large-scale credit card stealing operation in September. More recently, Google reported it was deployed in an attack against an aerospace organization in the U.S.
During the campaign investigated by Amazon, the AI agents were not always successful. For example, a 16-hour and 148-action effort to take control of a Redis server failed.
In a separate case targeting a university GPU server, the agents tried over 30,000 credential combinations over six hours but failed to brute-force their way in.
Finding and using a zero-day
According to Amazon, Cairn's AI agents found a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging application that uses AI to help researchers label medical images.
The flaw enabled the agents to write files to arbitrary locations on the server, and within 11 minutes, they went from mapping the application's API to exploiting the vulnerability.
In a subsequent session, the AI agents used the flaw to write a Python reverse shell to the sitecustomize.py
file that automatically loads when Python starts, then triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server.
After discovering the zero-day, the operator provided the agents with a proxy into a second university network running the same vulnerable software and directed them to target other machines.
Amazon reported the flaw to MONAI Label maintainers, and they released a security update to address it on November 18.
The researchers attributed the campaign to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language of the retrieved prompts, the activity timestamps, and the choice of targets.
Amazon also shared two IP addresses associated with the campaign, observed between September 8 and 10, 2026:
- 142[.]4.98.145
- 142[.]4.107.34
Amazon warned that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than security teams can react, urging organizations to rely more on automated defenses rather than manual investigations.

articles.title: NSA resumes normal operations following internal network disruptions
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Certain facilities remain under “Code Orange” for non-essential employees, meaning delayed openings and some must check in with their supervisors.
articles.full_text:
NSA resumes normal operations following internal network disruptions
The National Security Agency has mostly returned to business as usual after patches to a commonly-used programming language caused an internal communications network to crash for much of the week.
The spy agency is operating under “normal conditions, with exceptions” today, according to a Friday morning voicemail inbox recording for its workforce.
Certain facilities remain under “Code Orange” for non-essential employees, meaning delayed openings and some must check in with their supervisors.
The instructions come after three days of disruptions to NSANet, which allows employees to communicate classified information internally. The disruptions were attributed to maintenance affecting PHP, a ubiquitous programming language.
“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in a television interview earlier this week.
Workplace interruptions also occurred at NSA Georgia. Intelligence operations at that facility, focused on the Middle East, were not negatively impacted, according to two sources familiar with the situation.
The outages also did not curtail NSA’s ability to support President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, where he met with the leaders of China and Russia, these people said.
Administration officials have insisted the problems at the spy agency are not the result of a cyberattack and not connected to other IT woes that have impacted Microsoft products, airline travel and online banking services in recent days.
NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

articles.title: Cyber Director Cairncross out as White House resets cyber leadership
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Sean Cairncross is leaving the White House as Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, has been named the acting cyber czar.
articles.full_text:
Cyber Director Cairncross out as White House resets cyber leadership
U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving the White House post, creating upheaval among the Trump administration’s digital security leadership as the country wrestles with recent technology outages.
Axios first reported Cairncross’s exit. A White House official confirmed his departure, which reportedly had been pushed by President Donald Trump’s chief of staff Stephen Miller, who argued Cairncross lacked credentials to perform the job.
Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, has been named the acting cyber czar, which advises the president on cybersecurity matters and coordinates digital policy across the federal government.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on,” Davies, who the Senate confirmed for her role about a year ago, wrote on X.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Davies in social media posts on Thursday.
The high-profile departure comes amid a series of technology outages, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a global Microsoft Outlook outage and disruptions to the National Security Agency’s classified communications network. Administration officials have insisted that there are no indications a coordinated cyberattack caused the blackouts.
Cairncross, who previously was an executive at the Republican National Committee, was nominated by President Trump and confirmed last year. His office oversaw the crafting of the administration’s cyber strategy, all seven pages of which were released in March.
The brief document vowed to "detect, confront, and defeat cyber adversaries before they breach our networks and systems,” maintain an advantage in artificial intelligence and update federal networks.
His office also played a role in the administration’s executive order on AI.
Cairncross’ successor will need to be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
His exit came just hours after Michael LoSapio, the president’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), put his nomination in deep jeopardy by refusing to answer questions about who won the 2020 presidential election and denying the U.S. Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021.
Since LoSapio’s comments, Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Ron Wyden (D-OR) have publicly said they each would place a hold on his nomination to prevent him from being included in any en bloc package of nominees during the lame duck session of Congress.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

articles.title: Dozens of credit unions hit by supplier breach that went unnoticed for six weeks
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ireland’s Data Protection Commission told Recorded Future News on Thursday it had received more than 40 breach notifications from credit unions that used the Belfast-based company as a data processor.
articles.full_text:
Dozens of credit unions hit by supplier breach that went unnoticed for six weeks
Payment details belonging to members of more than 40 Irish credit unions have been accessed by hackers who exploited a vulnerability in the systems of software supplier Wellington IT.
Ireland’s Data Protection Commission told Recorded Future News on Thursday it had received more than 40 breach notifications from credit unions that used the Belfast-based company as a data processor.
With a customer base in Ireland and Wellington IT’s headquarters in Northern Ireland, a part of the United Kingdom, the incident straddles two jurisdictions.
The U.K.’s Information Commissioner’s Office told Recorded Future News it had not received a report from Wellington IT as of Thursday, but was “starting to see breach reports come through from Credit Unions,” suggesting the incident may also affect credit union members in the U.K.
Ireland’s Minister of State, Robert Troy, said in a statement the incident only affected payee details stored by members using credit union mobile banking apps operated by Wellington IT. Members who did not use the apps were unaffected, he said.
“At present, there is no evidence that members’ funds have been accessed or that any fraudulent activity involving members’ accounts has occurred,” said Troy.
The attack occurred in early October, David Malone, the chief executive of the Irish League of Credit Unions, told Ireland’s national broadcaster RTÉ.
Wellington said it closed the unidentified vulnerability itself on October 6, but that its initial investigation “did not identify that there was a data protection breach,” Malone said. The affected credit unions were not notified until November 16.
Robert Troy had previously described the delay as “simply not acceptable.” On Thursday, he said Wellington had brought in outside experts to determine “the exact number of accounts and users affected,” stressing that any information the company released publicly must be “accurate and verified.”
Wellington chief executive Colin Mitchell said the company notified customers “as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data.”
Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre said there was “no indication that member funds have been compromised or that unauthorised transactions have occurred.”
Wellington IT did not respond to a request for comment.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Lawmakers launch new AI safety caucus amid rising security concerns
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Seven of 26 founding members of the caucus are Republicans, a notable number given the White House’s steadfast opposition to regulating AI.
articles.full_text:
Lawmakers launch new AI safety caucus amid rising security concerns
A bipartisan group of than two dozen House lawmakers announced Thursday they are joining a new AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to confront the security risks posed by evolving and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence models.
The July breach of Hugging Face by an OpenAI agent that escaped a sandbox — and the subsequent Anthropic warning that its own AI models also broke out of testing environments to obtain unauthorized access to third-party organizations — have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” according to a press release from Rep. George Whitesides (D-CA), a caucus co-chair.
“As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems, and threats to national security.”
Whitesides and co-chairs Reps. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-VA) called for bipartisan collaboration to forge basic guardrails in the face of accelerating risks, citing Americans’ well-documented concerns about the technology.
Seven of 26 founding members of the caucus are Republicans, a notable number given the White House’s steadfast opposition to regulating AI. The caucus is focused on finding “targeted” solutions that will not imperil innovation, Whitesides said in a statement.
The lawmakers will push bipartisan legislation to augment AI safety and quickly respond to AI security incidents by gathering AI developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and help develop solutions, the press release said.
It will aggressively pursue relationships with outside experts who can help lawmakers navigate complicated AI policy decisions, focus on raising public awareness and give members outside of relevant committees the tools needed to contribute to relevant legislation and debate, according to the press release.
Midterm polling showed more than half of American voters considered AI a major issue, and 43% said they trust neither party to properly manage the issue, according to the press release.
“By automating vulnerability discovery and exploit development, AI tools have drastically reduced the technical skills required for offensive cyber operations,” a caucus one-pager said.
“As threat actors deploy these capabilities at scale, they pose acute risks to critical infrastructure, sensitive personal data, and financial sector stability.”
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop.
